To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

latch-up in a non-epitaxed CMOS inverter is mainly caused by electron injection from neighboring structures and can be avoided by the use of a p+ substrate, a thick oxide on the n-well, a thick oxide between the p+ substrate and the n-well and by the avoidance of n-wells in the neighborhood of the inverter.
the latch-up hardness is reduced by 10-30% due to electron injection from the n-channel and by 50-70% due to hole injection from the p-channel of the inverter.
latch-up is not a local but a global phenomenon, that it is not a single event but a process, and that its occurrence can be avoided by a careful choice of the layout and the bias conditions.

the latch-up problem of CMOS input and CMOS output stages.
the influence of neighboring CMOS structures on the latch up of an inverter.

the latch-up hardness in CMOS input and outputs stages, and we have found that latch-up can be avoided in the input and output stages by using a special layout and by using a special design for the input stage.

the influence of the latch-up neighborhood on the latch-up threshold of the inverter is negligible in the case of non-epitaxed VLSI CM OS.
the latch-up behavior of the inverter is determined by the sum of the latch-up behavior from each individual latch-up path.
the neighborhood effects are not as important as previously thought and that they can be minimized by a careful layout.

the influence of neighboring structures on latch-up hardness can be predicted with reasonable accuracy by the program BAM-BI, and that the latch-up hardness can easily be improved by a simple layout modification.

the neighborhood effects are not negligible in the design of latch-up hard CMOS input/output structures.
